title: Intrinsic Factors Affecting Injury Risk
description: How individual variables and psychological factors within the athlete influence their risk and severity of injury.
content_html:
What Are Intrinsic Factors?

Intrinsic factors are the internal characteristics that the athlete brings to every session — their age, fitness, nutrition, sleep quality, psychological state and injury history. Unlike extrinsic factors, intrinsic factors cannot always be controlled by a coach or facility manager; they require the athlete themselves to take responsibility for their own preparation and wellbeing. Intrinsic factors divide into individual variables and psychological factors.

Individual Variables

The specification lists ten individual variables. Gender influences injury risk because anatomical differences — including hip width, hormonal fluctuations and average muscle mass — mean that female athletes are statistically more susceptible to ACL injuries, while male athletes are more often involved in high-contact traumatic events. Age affects risk in both directions: younger athletes have developing bones and growth plates that are vulnerable to fracture and overuse; older athletes have reduced muscle elasticity, slower recovery rates and often longer histories of accumulated joint stress. Experience and technique/ability are closely related — poor technique places abnormal stress on muscles, tendons and joints, raising overuse and acute injury risk. Weight affects the load placed through joints on every step or landing; excessive body mass increases ground-reaction forces through the knees and hips, raising the risk of chronic conditions such as patellar tendonitis and shin splints.

Fitness levels interact with weight — a high fitness level means muscles, tendons and ligaments are better conditioned to withstand the demands of sport. Nutrition and hydration directly support muscle repair, bone density and energy availability; a poorly nourished athlete fatigues earlier and is more prone to both acute and chronic injury. Sleep is when the body repairs damaged tissue; chronic sleep deprivation impairs reaction time, coordination and pain tolerance, all of which elevate injury risk. Medical conditions — such as asthma, diabetes or a known cardiovascular issue — may limit the type or intensity of activity that is safe. Finally, previous or recurring injuries are one of the strongest predictors of future injury: scar tissue, reduced range of motion and compensatory movement patterns all increase vulnerability.

Key Fact

The ten individual variables are: gender, age, experience, weight, fitness levels, technique/ability, nutrition/hydration, medical conditions, sleep, and previous/recurring injuries. Variables can interact — for example, a participant's weight can directly influence their fitness levels and the stress placed through their joints.

Psychological Factors

An athlete's mental state is as important as their physical condition. The specification identifies five psychological factors. Motivation affects how hard an athlete trains and whether they take appropriate rest — over-motivated athletes may overtrain, dramatically increasing overuse injury risk. Arousal refers to the athlete's level of mental and physical activation; optimal arousal improves performance, but excessive arousal leads to muscular tension, impaired decision-making and reckless movement patterns that increase injury risk. Anxiety and stress have physical consequences: elevated cortisol impairs immune function and slows tissue healing; anxiety causes muscle tension that restricts normal movement and alters gait. Confidence works both ways — a highly confident athlete may attempt skills beyond their current ability, while a low-confidence athlete may hesitate at a critical moment, exposing them to injury through poor technique or mistimed actions.

Aggression

Direct aggression — physical force directed at an opponent outside the rules of the game — is a major cause of traumatic injury, both for the aggressor and the victim. The spec distinguishes this from channelled aggression, which is the controlled use of assertiveness within the rules of the sport (e.g. a hard but fair tackle in rugby). Understanding why aggression arises helps coaches manage it. The specification identifies five reasons: level of performance (frustration when performing below expectation), retaliation (responding to a foul or provocation), pressures to win from the performer, coach or spectators, decisions of officials (perceived injustice), and performance-enhancing drugs, some of which are linked to increased aggressive behaviour.

Key Fact

Direct aggression (physical force outside the rules) is a cause of injury; channelled aggression (assertiveness within the rules) is not. The five reasons for aggression in sport are: level of performance, retaliation, pressures to win, decisions of officials, and performance-enhancing drugs.

The specification includes mental strategies as intrinsic tools for managing psychological risk. Mental rehearsal involves the athlete vividly imagining a skill being performed correctly, which reinforces correct movement patterns and reduces the chance of technique breakdown under pressure. Imagery is a broader process of creating and using mental images — including visualising a safe, controlled landing or a measured tackle — to prepare the body and mind for the demands ahead. Selective attention involves filtering out distractions such as crowd noise or crowd-induced anxiety so the athlete can focus entirely on the task, reducing the likelihood of mistimed actions. These strategies are most closely linked to the psychological benefits of a warm up, which is where they are typically applied in practice.

The spec explicitly notes that individual variables can influence one another — this is where higher-level exam answers gain marks. For example, an athlete who has poor nutrition and inadequate sleep will also have lower fitness levels and impaired tissue healing — three variables compounding each other. A previous knee injury may lead a footballer to alter their running technique, which in turn places excess stress on the opposite hip, creating a new overuse injury site. Weight can directly influence fitness levels: higher body mass demands more cardiovascular effort during the same exercise intensity, leading to earlier fatigue. In 8-mark evaluate questions, demonstrating that intrinsic factors interact rather than acting in isolation will push an answer into the Mastering band.
exam_tip_html: When asked to "compare and contrast" intrinsic factors, structure your answer around both similarities and differences. For example, both poor nutrition and lack of sleep impair tissue repair and increase fatigue — but sleep deprivation additionally impairs reaction time and coordination, which are risk factors unique to that variable. Examiners reward answers that use the precise specification vocabulary ("previous/recurring injuries", "nutrition/hydration", "technique/ability") rather than informal language. For aggression questions, always distinguish direct from channelled aggression — failing to do so typically loses a mark.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The ten individual variables (gender, age, experience, weight, fitness levels, technique/ability, nutrition/hydration, medical conditions, sleep, previous/recurring injuries) all influence injury risk and can interact with one another in ways that compound risk.
  • Psychological factors — motivation, arousal, anxiety/stress, confidence and aggression — are intrinsic risk factors because they directly affect movement quality, decision-making and behaviour during sport.
  • Mental strategies (mental rehearsal, imagery, selective attention) can reduce psychological injury risk and are closely linked to the psychological benefits of a warm up covered earlier in this unit.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an intrinsic factor that influences injury risk?
A) The playing surface
B) The athlete's previous injuries
C) The quality of the coaching
D) The weather conditions
practice_questions.marks: B) The athlete's previous injuries [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two individual variables (1.2.1) that can influence the risk of injury for a sports performer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from the specification list: gender / age / experience / weight / fitness levels / technique/ability / nutrition/hydration / medical conditions / sleep / previous/recurring injuries. Answers that merely restate the same idea score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer's level of arousal can increase the risk of injury during competition.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "high arousal can increase injury risk"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "excessive arousal causes muscular tension and impairs decision-making, meaning athletes are more likely to make reckless movements or mistimed tackles"). A further developed explanation or second distinct mechanism scores 3 marks (e.g. add "very low arousal can also be dangerous — an under-aroused athlete may react too slowly to avoid a collision or fail to land safely from a jump"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by "direct aggression" in sport and give one example of how it can cause injury.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): direct aggression is physical force or violent behaviour directed at an opponent or person that falls outside the rules of the sport (2 marks for a clear developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement that aggression involves physical force).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a basketball player deliberately pushing an opponent to the floor after a disputed call — the pushed player falls awkwardly and sustains a wrist fracture, an injury that would not have occurred within normal play (2 marks for a specific, applied example with the injury mechanism identified; 1 mark for a vague example without the injury mechanism). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 17-year-old female sprinter has recently returned from a hamstring strain. She has been sleeping poorly due to pre-competition anxiety and has reduced her food intake to lose weight.

Discuss how the intrinsic factors present in this scenario increase the risk of re-injury.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two intrinsic factors with developed explanation and clear reference to the scenario. For example: the previous hamstring strain is the strongest predictor of re-injury — scar tissue is less elastic than the original muscle and she is likely still compensating in her movement patterns; poor sleep impairs tissue repair, meaning the original injury site has not fully healed; reduced nutrition means insufficient protein for muscle repair and lower energy availability, leading to earlier fatigue and loss of muscle control. The interaction between variables is noted (sleep and nutrition both impairing the same recovery process).
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two factors identified but explanation limited.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A male amateur rugby player has a high body mass index, a history of knee pain and poor match-day nutrition. He often arrives at training with low motivation and tends to play aggressively when his team is losing.

Evaluate the extent to which intrinsic factors are the main cause of injury risk for this performer, compared with extrinsic factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying multiple intrinsic factors (high body mass — increased joint load; previous knee pain — elevated re-injury risk; poor nutrition — fatigue and impaired healing; low motivation — reduced engagement with warm up and technique; direct aggression when losing — risk of foul play injury). Counter-argument identifies extrinsic factors (playing surface, quality of coaching, equipment, officiating standards) that independently or additionally create risk. Substantiated judgement — e.g. intrinsic factors are significant but interact with poor extrinsic provision, and neither category alone explains the full risk profile.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side, some applied to the scenario, an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the correct specification term for how accurately an athlete performs the movement patterns required by their sport?
Which type of aggression is defined as physical force directed at an opponent that falls outside the rules of the sport?
The specification states that a participant's _____ can directly influence their fitness levels, as greater body mass places more demand on the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems.
According to the specification, _____ is listed as a mental strategy (1.2.4) that can help athletes prepare for performance by mentally practising a skill before executing it.
Match each reason for aggression (1.2.3) to the correct description.
right: Perceived injustice — an unfair call or ruling triggers an aggressive response from a performer
Responding with aggression after being fouled or provoked by an opponent
Aggressive behaviour driven by expectation from a coach, teammates or crowd to achieve a result

glossary_terms.definition: Factors that originate from within the athlete's own body or mind and can increase the risk or severity of a sports injury.
The correctness of an athlete's movement patterns when performing sports skills, which directly affects the stress placed on muscles, tendons and joints.
The internal drive that pushes an athlete to train, compete and push through difficulty; can be intrinsic (from within) or extrinsic (from rewards or others).
An injury that has occurred before and may not have fully healed, making the same body part more susceptible to re-injury in the future.
